introduction-why-do-lines-form.core: Queues form whenever arrivals are variable and service takes time, even when average capacity exceeds average demand. Queueing theory relates arrival rate, service rate, utilisation and variability to waiting time, explaining why latency explodes as systems approach full utilisation and why burstiness hurts.

first_principles.problem: A service at 85% average CPU has terrible p99 latency, and the team doesn't understand why.
derivation: Measure **arrival rate λ** and **service rate μ**.

analogy.title: A supermarket checkout
analogy.story: Even if the cashier can handle the day's customers on average, clumps of shoppers create queues.
analogy.breaks: Shoppers can leave; requests wait unless timed out or shed.

example.title: Same average, different waits
flow: Steady arrivals at 80% load: short waits
Bursty arrivals at 80% load: long waits
Variance, not just load, drives queues

check.q: Why do queues form even when average capacity exceeds demand?
check.a: Arrival and service times vary, so bursts temporarily exceed capacity.

littles-law-the-golden-rule.core: Little's law: L = λ × W. The average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends in it. It holds for any stable system regardless of distribution, so you can derive concurrency, queue length or latency from the other two, e.g. needed threads or connections.

first_principles.problem: A team can't estimate how many database connections a service needs.
truths: The law needs no distribution assumptions.
Stable systems obey it on average.
derivation: Diagnose **queue growth** (W rising at fixed λ).

analogy.title: A coffee shop's occupancy
analogy.story: If 30 customers arrive per hour and each stays 20 minutes, about 10 are inside at any time.
analogy.breaks: Coffee shop capacity is visible; in-flight requests are hidden unless measured.

check.q: A service handles 500 req/s with 200 ms latency. How many requests are in flight on average?

utilization-how-busy-are-we.core: Utilisation ρ = λ/μ is the fraction of time a server is busy. In an M/M/1 queue, average waiting grows as ρ/(1−ρ): at 50% you wait about 1 service time, at 90% about 9, at 99% about 99. Running hot saves money but destroys tail latency, so target utilisation must reflect latency goals and variability.

first_principles.problem: Finance wants servers at 95% utilisation, and engineering knows latency will explode.

analogy.title: Motorway traffic
analogy.story: Up to a point traffic flows; near full capacity, small additions cause huge jams.
analogy.breaks: Roads have physical lanes; servers can be added within minutes.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: The last 10% of utilisation is very expensive in latency.

check.q: In an M/M/1 queue, how does waiting time change from 80% to 90% utilisation?
check.a: It more than doubles, from about 4 to about 9 service times.

kingmans-formula-the-hockey-stick-curve.core: Kingman's formula approximates waiting time for general queues: W ≈ (ρ/(1−ρ)) × ((Ca² + Cs²)/2) × service time, where Ca and Cs are coefficients of variation of arrivals and service. Latency rises like a hockey stick near full utilisation, and variability multiplies it, so reducing variance helps as much as adding capacity.

first_principles.problem: A service with highly variable request sizes has awful latency at only 70% utilisation.
truths: Utilisation and variability both drive waits.
derivation: Reduce **Cs**: split large jobs, separate queues for big/small.

analogy.title: A queue where some customers bring 100 items
analogy.story: Variable basket sizes make the line far worse than steady small baskets.
analogy.breaks: Supermarkets add express lanes physically; systems can route by request size dynamically.

example.title: Separating heavy requests
flow: Mixed queue: Cs = 3 → p99 1.8 s at 70%
Separate pools for exports vs page views
Page view queue Cs = 0.5 → p99 120 ms

check.q: According to Kingman, what two factors multiply queueing delay?
check.a: Utilisation (ρ/(1−ρ)) and variability of arrivals and service times.

the-universal-scalability-law-usl.core: The Universal Scalability Law models throughput as C(N) = N / (1 + α(N−1) + βN(N−1)), where α is contention (serialised parts, Amdahl) and β is coherency (crosstalk, synchronising state). With β > 0, adding nodes eventually reduces throughput. Fitting USL to load tests predicts the peak and guides architecture changes.

first_principles.problem: Adding servers past 32 makes a database cluster slower, not faster.
truths: Coordination costs grow with pairs of nodes.

analogy.title: Adding cooks to a kitchen
analogy.story: More cooks help until they queue for the stove (contention) and spend time coordinating (coherency).
analogy.breaks: Kitchens have fixed stoves; software can remove shared resources by redesign.

example.title: Fitting a cluster
flow: Sharding hot table cuts β → peak 120

check.q: What does the β (coherency) term in USL represent?
check.a: The cost of keeping nodes in sync, which grows with pairs of nodes and can make throughput decline.
